summary: PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body
description:
### Summary

PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker.

### Details

FastCGI and LSAPI connections can carry more than one request. Before accepting another request on the same connection, PHP must either consume the previous request body or close the connection.

Opening `php://input` creates a request-body stream, but PHP reads its contents lazily. During request shutdown, PHP incorrectly treated the existence of this stream as evidence that the body had already been handled and skipped the normal cleanup that discards unread input.

An attacker can combine this behaviour with a malformed `multipart/form-data` body that makes PHP's multipart parser stop at a predictable position. If the application then opens `php://input` without reading it to the end, attacker-controlled body bytes remain in the current backend request. This can occur in request frameworks that create an input stream before routing or authentication, even when the selected endpoint does not use the body.

When `FCGI_KEEP_CONN` is enabled, PHP-FPM preserves the connection and starts parsing another FastCGI request. The vulnerable implementation discarded its knowledge that it was still inside an `FCGI_STDIN` record, so a FastCGI message placed at the appropriate body offset was accepted as a new request. The front end never created or authorised this request.

The forged request controls FastCGI parameters including `SCRIPT_FILENAME`, `REMOTE_ADDR` and `PHP_ADMIN_VALUE`. If the attacker knows the path of an existing PHP script, they can set `allow_url_include=1` and `auto_prepend_file=php://input`, causing the forged request's own input to be executed as PHP. The changed administrator settings can also remain active for later requests served by the same worker. The shared request-cleanup error also affects LSAPI's persistent request lifecycle, but LSAPI does not use this FastCGI parameter mechanism.

The issue was introduced with lazy `php://input` handling in PHP 5.6.0. The fix drains input according to whether the body was fully consumed, independently of whether a `php://input` stream exists. PHP-FPM additionally closes a connection instead of accepting another request when the previous FastCGI input record is incomplete.

### Impact

Exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens `php://input` without reading it fully. Relevant configurations include nginx with `fastcgi_keep_conn on`, Apache `mod_proxy_fcgi` with `enablereuse=on`, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated PHP-FPM attack.

For PHP-FPM, successful exploitation can execute attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. It can also dispatch an existing PHP script outside the routes exposed by the front end, supply a forged client address to application access controls, or change administrator-level PHP settings for subsequent requests. The attack crosses the HTTP-to-PHP backend trust boundary using a single request. It does not require memory corruption, knowledge of memory addresses or a race condition.

For LSAPI, the shared cleanup error can leave body bytes on a persistent backend connection, desynchronising the request stream and disrupting subsequent requests. The `PHP_ADMIN_VALUE` chain used for PHP-FPM is not an LSAPI parameter path, so this advisory does not establish arbitrary code execution through LSAPI.

### Affected versions

The affected code has been present since PHP 5.6.0. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, disable backend connection reuse on the affected front end: leave nginx `fastcgi_keep_conn` disabled, leave Apache `enablereuse` disabled, or configure another FastCGI front end to close its backend connection after every request.

Reading `php://input` to the end before completing every request prevents the demonstrated unread-body condition, but error paths, resource exhaustion and application shutdown can make this unreliable as the sole mitigation. Do not expose PHP-FPM or LSAPI listeners directly to untrusted networks.

summary: Session serializer mismatch can lead to remote code execution
description:
### Summary

PHP's session upload progress feature can write attacker-controlled data using one session serialization format and later read it using another. A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker.

This is a configuration-dependent deserialization issue, separate from the stale global state vulnerability in CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp). Session upload progress was introduced in PHP 5.4.0, so older unsupported releases may also be affected.

### Details

The affected setup has the following conditions:

- Session upload progress is enabled, and an attacker can submit a multipart upload to a context using `php_binary` or `php_serialize` as its session serializer.
- A later or concurrent operation can access the same stored session, using the same session ID and the `php` serializer.
- For code execution, the reading application has a suitable deserialization gadget chain available.

The mismatch can arise when an application changes `session.serialize_handler` to `php` before calling `session_start()`. It can also arise between separate applications, pools, virtual hosts, or command-line processes with different fixed INI settings. With the `files` handler, this requires the same session storage directory, the same session ID, and permissions allowing both sides to access that file. Separate FPM pools do not automatically provide separate session storage. A runtime configuration change is not required, but workers using the same serializer do not create this mismatch.

During multipart processing, PHP appends the submitted `PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS` value to an upload-progress session key and persists it. The `php` format separates each key from its serialized value with `|`. The other formats represent keys differently. If their output is read as `php`, an attacker-supplied delimiter can cause bytes inside the key to be passed to PHP's unserialization machinery.

Objects may be created and their deserialization or destruction callbacks invoked before trailing data causes the session decoder to reject the record. The 127-byte key limit in `php_binary` does not prevent payloads that span multiple session records.

### Impact

Successful exploitation can cause remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial of service. The report includes command execution using a Guzzle object gadget on PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Command execution was also reproduced with a Monolog 2.11.1 gadget using a `php_serialize` writer and a `php` reader. Exploitability depends on the shared session configuration, access to the writing and reading paths, and the classes available to the reader.

An application that never changes its serializer at runtime can still be affected if another application or process writes incompatible data into the same session store.

### Affected versions

Session upload progress has been affected since it was introduced in PHP 5.4.0. The variant that uses a `php_serialize` writer requires PHP 5.5.4 or later. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. The fix disables session upload progress by default and rejects runtime changes to session settings, including `session.serialize_handler`, while upload progress is enabled. Keeping the feature disabled removes the upload-progress attack path described in this advisory. Check for existing configuration that explicitly enables it, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.

**If session upload progress is explicitly enabled in any application or pool, all readers and writers of the session data it can access must use the same `session.serialize_handler`, even after the update.** The fix does not enforce matching serializers across separate configurations.

For installations that need the feature, check the effective settings in php.ini, FPM pools, virtual hosts, application overrides, and command-line jobs. Isolate session storage when applications require different formats. When changing an existing store's format, migrate or expire its old records instead of reading them with the new serializer.

Otherwise, keep `session.upload_progress.enabled=0` in every configuration that can write to the affected session store. Set this administratively before request input is processed. Calling `ini_set()` from the application is too late. Do not rely on upload-progress cleanup to prevent a concurrent read.

summary: SOAP use-after-free when processing DTD entity references
description:
### Summary

PHP's SOAP extension can read freed memory while processing XML containing a document type definition (DTD) and an entity reference in an attribute value. An unauthenticated attacker who can send a crafted request to an exposed SOAP endpoint can crash the PHP process handling it. Applications that load attacker-controlled WSDL or imported schema documents can also be affected.

### Details

While cleaning up a parsed XML document, PHP frees the DTD even though attribute values can still refer to content it owns. Processing those attributes can then access freed memory. Removing the DTD also bypasses the SOAP server's normal rejection of documents containing a DTD.

The fix keeps the DTD alive for as long as the XML document needs it and restores the existing SOAP DTD check. The issue predates the changes made for [CVE-2026-91765](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-rgrp-mwpx-f6rm) and affects earlier releases in all supported PHP branches.

### Impact

Exploitation requires the SOAP extension and an application that processes attacker-controlled SOAP XML, WSDL or schema content. Authentication does not protect an endpoint if the application parses the SOAP request before authenticating it.

A crafted document can crash the PHP worker or process, and repeated requests can disrupt service. The original report also described corrupted type information after freed memory was reused. Disclosure of sensitive process memory and arbitrary code execution have not been confirmed.

### Affected versions

SOAP server requests have been affected since PHP 5.6.0. The same cleanup has applied to WSDL and schema documents since PHP 5.0.0, but loading an untrusted WSDL or schema is not considered a security issue. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, restrict access to affected SOAP endpoints or disable them where practical. Load WSDL and imported schemas only from trusted, controlled sources.

If untrusted SOAP requests must be accepted, reject documents containing a DTD before they reach the SOAP extension. Any such filter must correctly handle the XML encodings and request-body transformations accepted by the application. A simple text search is not a complete mitigation.

summary: Double free during DOM XML serialization
description:
### Summary

PHP's modern DOM XML serializer can incorrectly share ownership of a generated namespace prefix between an element and its descendant. An application that calls `saveXml()` on attacker-controlled XML or HTML can consequently use and free the same allocation more than once, which can crash the PHP process.

### Details

`Dom\XMLDocument` and `Dom\HTMLDocument` maintain a namespace-prefix map while serializing a document as XML. The serializer can generate a prefix for an attribute whose namespace has no usable prefix. Descendants initially share the ancestor's map and use copy-on-write when adding another candidate prefix for an existing namespace URI.

The vulnerable copy-on-write path duplicates the candidate list but leaves the copied pointers marked as owned. Destroying the descendant's map therefore frees a generated prefix that remains referenced by the ancestor. A later sibling can access that freed value, and destroying the ancestor's map frees the same allocation again. The fix marks generated-prefix pointers copied into descendant lists as borrowed.

Valid input can establish this state by combining namespaced attributes, nested namespace declarations and a later sibling. The input does not need to be malformed. The HTML path requires only a crafted document followed by `Dom\HTMLDocument::saveXml()`. For `Dom\XMLDocument`, the same state can arise when ordinary application code adds a namespaced attribute and the supplied document declares another prefix for that namespace.

### Impact

A remote attack requires an application to parse attacker-controlled XML or HTML using the modern DOM API and then serialize it with `saveXml()`. Applications that do not XML-serialize untrusted documents are not affected by that attack path.

The demonstrated impact is memory corruption and denial of service through a PHP process crash. Corrupting ZendMM's free list may allow later allocations in the same request to alias, but turning that into type confusion or code execution requires application-specific allocation control and has not been demonstrated through realistic application code. No confidentiality or integrity impact has been established.

Repeated requests can terminate PHP workers and reduce or exhaust an application's worker pool.

### Affected versions

The affected code was introduced in PHP 8.4.0 together with the `Dom\XMLDocument` and `Dom\HTMLDocument` classes and their XML serializer. The legacy `DOMDocument` class does not use this serializer. PHP 8.3 and earlier are not affected.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, avoid calling `saveXml()` on attacker-controlled `Dom\XMLDocument` or `Dom\HTMLDocument` instances. For HTML documents where XML output is not required, `saveHtml()` avoids the affected XML serializer. Process isolation and worker restart limits can contain individual crashes but do not remove the vulnerable behavior.

summary: SOAP information disclosure through malformed array dimensions
description:
### Summary

PHP's SOAP extension can expose a small amount of uninitialized heap memory when processing an encoded array with an invalid `arraySize` value. An attacker can supply a crafted SOAP request or response that causes the decoded array to contain an unexpected integer key. The value reaches the attacker if the application returns or otherwise exposes that array.

### Details

An empty, whitespace-only or non-numeric `arraySize` can describe no dimensions. PHP nevertheless reads the first array position, which has not been initialized. With PHP's default memory allocator, the read falls within a small allocated block and can return four bytes of unrelated heap data. That value is then used as an array key. When the default allocator is disabled, AddressSanitizer reports an out-of-bounds heap read.

The fix treats a size containing no dimensions as a one-dimensional array. It also covers array dimensions read from WSDL definitions. The vulnerable behaviour is present in all supported PHP branches.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can trigger the issue through a SOAP endpoint that accepts the crafted input. A malicious or compromised SOAP server can also supply an affected response to `SoapClient`.

The demonstrated impact is limited information disclosure when the application exposes the decoded array. Simply accepting the request does not guarantee that the value is returned to the attacker. The demonstrated case does not crash or corrupt memory with PHP's default allocator. Arbitrary code execution has not been demonstrated.

### Affected versions

The affected code has been present since PHP 5.0.0. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, restrict access to affected SOAP endpoints and use trusted SOAP services and WSDL definitions.

Where requests or responses can be validated before they reach the SOAP extension, reject encoded arrays whose `arraySize` contains no valid dimension. Avoid returning unvalidated decoded arrays to untrusted clients. These measures reduce exposure but do not replace the parser fix.

summary: PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass via algorithm downgrade
description:
### Summary

An attacker who can modify an OpenSSL-signed Phar archive without changing its trusted public key can make PHP accept arbitrary archive contents. The attacker changes the archive's signature type to a keyless hash such as SHA-256 and replaces the OpenSSL signature with a matching digest. Applications that execute the archive may then run attacker-controlled PHP code.

### Details

PHP stores an OpenSSL signature in the Phar archive, but obtains the verification key from a separate `<archive>.pubkey` file. For the native phar format, the archive controls the signature type through the four bytes before the `GBMB` magic. Tar- and zip-based phars control it through the first four bytes of `.phar/signature.bin`.

The verifier treats this type as authoritative when selecting the verification method. Only the OpenSSL signature types read and use `<archive>.pubkey`. MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 compare a digest that anyone can recompute. An attacker can therefore replace the archive contents and OpenSSL signature, select SHA-256 and satisfy `phar.require_hash=1` without possession of the private key. The trusted public key is not consulted.

Native, tar- and zip-based executable phars are affected. Explicitly signed tar- and zip-based `PharData` archives use the same verification path. This behaviour has been present since OpenSSL Phar signatures were introduced in PHP 5.3.0. The fix rejects a non-OpenSSL signature when an adjacent `.pubkey` file indicates that OpenSSL verification is expected. Archives without such a sidecar retain their existing signature behaviour.

### Impact

Exploitation requires the application to rely on an OpenSSL-signed Phar with a public key installed through a trusted channel, an attacker able to alter or replace the archive but not that public key, and the application subsequently loading the archive. Executing the modified archive can run attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the affected process, compromising its data and availability.

The `.pubkey` file is PHP's external trust anchor and is not embedded or pinned in the Phar. If an attacker can also remove or replace it, they can already provide an archive signed with their own OpenSSL key. the fix does not protect that deployment. `phar.require_hash` alone provides corruption detection and does not authenticate keyless signatures.

### Affected versions

The affected code has been present since PHP 5.3.0. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Obtain the publisher's public key through an authenticated channel and install it as `<archive>.pubkey` with permissions that prevent the archive update or download path from removing or replacing it. If the key cannot be protected independently, verify the archive using another mechanism that pins a trusted key before PHP loads it.

summary: PHP-CGI out-of-bounds read and write during PATH_INFO correction
description:
### Summary

The PHP CGI binary (`php-cgi`) can access memory outside the supplied path information when a web server passes inconsistent script and path values. Depending on the request and configuration, an unauthenticated attacker may be able to crash the PHP process, expose process memory, or corrupt memory.

This affects `php-cgi` in both CGI and FastCGI mode when `cgi.fix_pathinfo=1`, the default. PHP-FPM and PHP running as an Apache module are not affected.

### Details

The problem occurs when PHP removes a trailing path from `SCRIPT_FILENAME`, or from `PATH_TRANSLATED` in a redirected CGI request, but the supplied `PATH_INFO` is shorter than the path being removed. A present but empty `PATH_INFO` can also trigger the problem. This requires particular web server mappings; using CGI, FastCGI, or URL rewriting alone is not enough.

In `init_request_info()`, PHP calculates the replacement `PATH_INFO` by subtracting the length of the removed suffix from the end of the supplied value. If the suffix is longer, the resulting pointer lies before the `PATH_INFO` buffer. Subsequent path correction can read, write and copy memory through this invalid pointer. The fix checks the lengths before deriving the pointer and skips the rewrite when no valid replacement exists.

#### Apache CGI example

A legitimate configuration that can produce these values is a legacy Apache CGI installation using `Action`, combined with a rewrite to an absolute filesystem path. For example, this virtual-host configuration routes a short public URL to a longer route handled by an existing `/srv/site/index.php`:

```apache
DocumentRoot "/srv/site"
ScriptAlias /cgi-bin/php "/usr/local/bin/php-cgi"

AddHandler php-script .php
Action php-script /cgi-bin/php

<Directory "/srv/site">
    AcceptPathInfo On
</Directory>

RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule "^/news/(.*)$" "/srv/site/index.php/content/articles/$1" [L]
```

This fragment assumes an otherwise working Apache CGI installation with the required modules and access permissions. The `Action` arrangement is described in the [PHP CGI installation documentation](https://www.php.net/manual/en/security.cgi-bin.force-redirect.php).

A request for `/news/x` can then reach PHP with:

```text
PATH_INFO       = /news/x
PATH_TRANSLATED = /srv/site/index.php/content/articles/x
REDIRECT_URL    = /news/x
```

PHP finds the existing `index.php`, but the remaining `/content/articles/x` is longer than the original `/news/x`. Attempting to reconcile these values triggers the invalid memory access. This was reproduced through an actual HTTP request with Apache 2.4.58 and an unmodified PHP CGI binary. An `Alias` that maps `/news` to `/srv/site/index.php/content/articles` produced the same result.

The ordinary `Action` setup, a conventional rewrite to `index.php`, and a rewrite to the URL `/index.php/content/articles/x` did not trigger the issue in these tests. The vulnerable example is a valid routing configuration, but it does not imply that typical Apache PHP installations are affected.

#### Other FastCGI front ends

A front end can also expose the issue if it builds `SCRIPT_FILENAME` from an unsplit request path while supplying a shorter or empty `PATH_INFO`. Review custom FastCGI parameter mappings and configurations that forward requests without checking that the selected script exists. For nginx, this includes checking how [`fastcgi_split_path_info`](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_fastcgi_module.html#fastcgi_split_path_info), `SCRIPT_FILENAME`, `PATH_INFO`, and any `try_files` check work together. A correctly split and validated script path avoids this form of the issue.

An exposed `php-cgi` FastCGI listener also allows an untrusted client to supply these parameters directly. PHP-FPM remains unaffected.

### Impact

- **Denial of service:** a single unauthenticated request can crash the `php-cgi` process handling it. Crashes were reproduced on default, non-debug builds of PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.
- **Information disclosure:** unrelated memory can appear in `$_SERVER['PATH_INFO']` or `PATH_TRANSLATED`. This may include other request parameters or values added by the front end. Disclosure to the attacker depends on the application returning these values or making them available through logs or other output.
- **Memory corruption:** PHP can overwrite memory during path correction. Code execution has been claimed, but has not been confirmed.

### Affected versions

The out-of-bounds read has been present since PHP 4.3.0 and the out-of-bounds write since PHP 5.2.4. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. As a workaround, set `cgi.fix_pathinfo=0` in the configuration used by `php-cgi`, and check that the application's routing still works.

Alternatively, correct the web server mapping so that the path PHP uses identifies the existing script and any additional path information is consistent. For the Apache example above, rewriting to the URL instead of the absolute filesystem path avoided the issue:

```apache
RewriteRule "^/news/(.*)$" "/index.php/content/articles/$1" [PT,L]
```

See Apache's documentation for the [`PT` rewrite flag](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/rewrite/flags.html#flag_pt). Other rewrites and aliases can affect the result, so verify the complete configuration. Direct access to a FastCGI listener should also be restricted to trusted front ends.

summary: PHP-FPM status endpoint XSS via unescaped user and script fields
description:
### Summary

PHP-FPM can include attacker-controlled request metadata without escaping it in the full status response. An unauthenticated attacker can place HTML or JavaScript in a worker's scoreboard entry and execute it in the browser of an operator who later views the full HTML status page. The attacker does not need access to the status endpoint.

### Details

The earlier fix for [CVE-2026-6735](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-7qg2-v9fj-4mwv) escaped the request URI and query string, but left the request method, authentication user and script filename unescaped in the per-process status output. These values are stored in the PHP-FPM scoreboard and later inserted into HTML, XML and JSON responses without the encoding required by each format.

The most direct attack uses the username from an HTTP Basic authentication header. When the front end forwards this header to PHP-FPM, PHP can decode and store the supplied username even if the application does not use Basic authentication. The scoreboard retains up to 31 bytes of the username, which is enough for an HTML element with a JavaScript event handler. A request to an ordinary PHP script in the pool can therefore plant a payload that runs when another user opens the status endpoint with `full&html`. The value remains in that worker's scoreboard entry until it is replaced by a later request.

The script filename provides another injection path when an attacker can influence the filename recorded by FPM, including configurations using `cgi.fix_pathinfo=0`. Ordinary web servers restrict the characters accepted in request methods, so the request-method field does not by itself establish the same HTTP attack path. Unescaped quotes or markup in these fields can also corrupt JSON or XML status responses and interfere with monitoring consumers.

The fix applies a common, format-appropriate escaping helper to the request method, request URI, query string, authentication user and script filename before rendering the full status response. A separate client-side injection issue in the bundled `status.html` dashboard is tracked in [GHSA-q8fm-p8fx-h6r6](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-q8fm-p8fx-h6r6).

### Impact

Exploitation requires an enabled PHP-FPM status endpoint, a request path through which attacker-controlled metadata reaches the affected pool, and a user or tool that renders the full status data as HTML. For the authentication-user attack, the front end must forward the Basic authentication header to FPM. Restricting access to the status endpoint does not prevent an attacker from planting the payload through a separate application request.

Successful exploitation runs JavaScript in the status page's origin. It can expose request URIs, query strings and other information shown on the status page. If the page shares an origin with the application, the script can also act with the viewing user's session and read data available to that origin, including cookies that are not protected by `HttpOnly`. Malformed XML or JSON can additionally disrupt status parsing and monitoring.

### Affected versions

The affected status output has been present since PHP 5.3.9. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. As a temporary workaround, disable the PHP-FPM status endpoint or prevent use of its full HTML output. If full status data is required, use a consumer that validates the response and treats all field values as untrusted text. Restricting status access to trusted operators remains useful, but is not a complete mitigation because those operators can receive payloads planted by other clients.

summary: Timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution
description:
### Summary

PHP can retain a reference to a freed timezone cache when a diagnostic is written to a PHP error log file during process startup. A later diagnostic during early request initialization can access the freed cache before it is reset. On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker.

### Details

PHP formats file-based error log timestamps using the configured timezone. In a non-thread-safe build, a diagnostic emitted during module startup can cause PHP to allocate the timezone cache in temporary startup memory. That memory is released at the end of startup, but the internal reference to the cache remains until the date extension initializes the first request. An earlier diagnostic, such as the warning produced when request input exceeds `max_input_vars`, can therefore read or modify a freed hash table. The released memory may already contain attacker-controlled request data.

The startup diagnostic must occur late enough that subsequent initialization does not clear the cached reference. Confirmed examples include an invalid `date.timezone` value and a warning or deprecation caused by session configuration. The diagnostic must actually be written through PHP's file-based `error_log` path. FPM's own error log does not by itself meet this condition.

In FPM and Apache mod_php, workers can inherit the stale reference from the parent process. The vulnerable window lasts until a worker completes its first normal request. Newly created or recycled workers can encounter the same condition. A crafted HTTP request has been shown to crash an FPM worker using the default `max_input_vars` value and ordinary nginx header limits. The issue has also been reproduced with CGI.

A separate local FPM proof demonstrated native command execution with known runtime addresses. It uses early HTTP Basic credential decoding to replace the stale cache, then reuses request-data allocations and triggers their destruction while `$_REQUEST` is constructed. That particular chain requires additional configuration, including `auto_globals_jit=0` and cookies in `request_order`, a suitable heap layout, and an Authorization header larger than nginx's default per-header limit. These are conditions of the demonstrated exploit, not general requirements of the underlying memory-corruption flaw. Other exploitation paths may be possible.

Native command execution has also been demonstrated in Apache mod_php. Besides the same GET/COOKIE chain, Apache has a separate path when request startup fails before the cache is reset. Request cleanup can destroy the forged cache and invoke an attacker-controlled destructor. The demonstrated variant uses a POST that exceeds a configured 2 MB PHP memory limit and requires known runtime addresses, a suitable heap layout, and a larger allowed Authorization header. It does not require cookies or changes to `auto_globals_jit` or `request_order`. ASLR remained enabled during these proofs. A remote ASLR bypass is plausible, although a complete independent bypass has not been demonstrated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker may be able to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. The trigger requires a suitable startup diagnostic, PHP error logging to a file, and an early request diagnostic in a fresh worker. Code execution has been demonstrated locally in FPM and Apache mod_php with known addresses and additional configuration assumptions. Successful exploitation does not require application-level code execution or attacker control of `PHP_VALUE` or `PHP_ADMIN_VALUE`.

### Affected versions

The affected code has been present since PHP 5.3.18 and 5.4.8. An earlier form of it was present in PHP 5.2.10, 5.2.12 to 5.2.17 and 5.3.0 to 5.3.8. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, or 8.5.13 when the corresponding release is available. The fix formats error log timestamps in UTC outside a fully initialized active request, avoiding use of request-local timezone state at unsafe points in the lifecycle.

Until an update can be deployed, correct configuration errors and deprecated settings that produce startup diagnostics, then restart the PHP master process and all workers. Sending PHP errors to a suitable logging destination that does not use this file-timestamp path, such as syslog, also avoids the demonstrated trigger. Changing `$_REQUEST` or cookie settings is not a complete mitigation. The demonstrated Apache cleanup path does not require those settings.

summary: Partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution
description:
### Summary

PHP's file-based session handler can leave a session file containing parts of two different serialized sessions if a write is interrupted. An attacker who can influence the session contents and interrupt a replacement write may be able to make PHP deserialize attacker-controlled objects when the session is next opened. A suitable object gadget chain in the application can turn this into remote code execution.

This affects the `files` session save handler, which is PHP's default. The issue is not limited to session upload progress or PHP 8.6.

### Details

When updating a session, `ps_files_write()` writes the new serialized data into the existing file. The vulnerable implementation does not clear the existing contents before every write. If the operation stops after replacing only part of the file, the result can contain a prefix of the new session followed by a suffix of the old one. The file lock prevents competing session operations from accessing the file during the write, but does not make an interrupted write atomic.

PHP's session decoders use its unserialization machinery to restore session values. Carefully arranged old and new data can cause the combined file to be interpreted differently from either original session. Bytes that were previously part of an ordinary string can become serialized object data. A later `session_start()` or another session-reading operation can then create those objects and invoke their deserialization behavior.

Session upload progress provides one way for a remote client to influence stored session data through multipart uploads. The same underlying problem can arise when an application stores large user-controlled strings in a session. In threaded PHP builds, a hard memory-limit failure in another thread can terminate the process while the session write is in progress. This provides a way to influence where the write stops.

The fix truncates the session file to zero before writing the replacement data and aborts the write if truncation fails. An interrupted write can still lose session data, but it can no longer retain the old suffix that enables this attack.

### Impact

Successful exploitation can execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker. It requires attacker influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. The issue can also corrupt session state. Authentication requirements depend on how the application exposes the affected session operations.

Other session storage implementations are not affected by this specific file-write defect, although their own handling of interrupted updates must be considered separately.

### Affected versions

The affected code has been present since PHP 4.1.0. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. As a temporary measure, disable `session.upload_progress.enabled` administratively if the feature is not needed, and limit the amount of untrusted data stored in sessions. Disabling upload progress removes that input path but does not fix applications that independently store attacker-controlled session data.

A session storage backend that replaces records atomically can avoid this file-write defect. The PHP update remains the recommended fix for applications using the built-in `files` handler.

summary: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution
description:
### Summary

PHP can access freed memory when collecting the arguments of a method handled by `__call()` or `__callStatic()` for a backtrace. On PHP 8.5 and later, an unauthenticated attacker may be able to trigger this through a crafted request that causes a fatal error while the application enters such a method. Successful exploitation can execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker.

The demonstrated remote attack requires `fatal_error_backtraces=1` and `zend.exception_ignore_args=0`. Fatal error backtraces are enabled by default in PHP 8.5. PHP's built-in default also includes arguments, but `php.ini-production` sets `zend.exception_ignore_args=1` and prevents this attack path.

### Details

Applications and frameworks commonly use `__call()` and `__callStatic()` to forward method calls to another object, including logging facades, database interfaces and service proxies. Before PHP enters the actual magic method, it briefly represents the requested method as a separate call. A backtrace taken during this interval can collect values left behind by an earlier call instead of the current arguments. Some of those values can refer to memory that has already been freed.

The demonstrated attack submits crafted JSON to an import endpoint that processes the body and then logs it through a magic static method. The request is sized so that constructing a logging argument crosses `memory_limit`. PHP 8.5.12 introduced delayed handling of this allocation failure, allowing the fatal error to be reported while the magic method call is being entered. If fatal error backtraces include arguments, PHP can then treat request-controlled bytes in reused memory as live values. Processing or releasing the backtrace can corrupt memory or transfer control to an attacker-chosen address.

Fatal error backtraces were introduced in PHP 8.5.0. An execution time limit expiring during the same interval is another possible trigger. PHP 8.2–8.4 contain the underlying backtrace error, but reaching it requires a PCNTL signal handler or another component to inspect an interrupted call. No attacker-controlled remote trigger has been established for those branches. They are therefore outside this advisory’s affected version range.

### Impact

Remote code execution has been confirmed on PHP 8.5 and later. Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. The demonstrated code execution chain also requires knowledge of usable memory addresses despite address space randomisation. Other attempts can crash the worker or produce an ordinary resource limit error.

Potentially relevant paths include [Laravel facades](https://github.com/laravel/framework/blob/v13.40.0/src/Illuminate/Support/Facades/Facade.php#L356) and [Magento guest shipping estimation](https://github.com/magento/magento2/blob/2.4.9/app/code/Magento/Quote/etc/webapi.xml#L169). These examples establish that existing applications reach magic method calls, but exploitation of a complete Laravel or Magento installation has not been demonstrated.

The presence of a framework, a magic method, or a large request body alone does not establish exploitability. The attacker does not need to upload PHP code or invoke a method name of their choosing if the application's existing request path reaches a suitable call. Authentication requirements depend on that path.

### Affected versions

The attack path was introduced in PHP 8.5.0 by fatal error backtraces, which collect the arguments of every active call whenever a fatal error is reported. PHP 8.2 to 8.4 contain the underlying backtrace error but have no known remote trigger and are outside the affected range.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13 when it becomes available. As an immediate workaround for the fatal error attack, set `zend.exception_ignore_args=1` in the configuration used by the affected PHP workers and restart them. On PHP 8.5 and later, setting `fatal_error_backtraces=0` also prevents this attack path. Check the effective configuration, including FPM pool settings and application overrides. Changing only the CLI configuration is insufficient.

Setting `display_errors=0` does not prevent PHP from constructing the backtrace. Request-size limits and avoiding expensive processing or logging of untrusted bodies can reduce exposure, but are not a complete substitute for the configuration workaround or update. Extensions that independently inspect interrupted calls should also be reviewed.

summary: Incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization for oversized input
description:
### Summary

PHP's RFC 3986 URI implementation can return an incorrect string when a very large URI is converted back to text. An application that accepts attacker-controlled URI data and has enough memory to process it may receive a truncated or invalid URI instead of an error. Processing these inputs can also exhaust memory or terminate the PHP process.

This affects the `Uri\Rfc3986\Uri` class introduced in PHP 8.5.0. The legacy `parse_url()` function and the separate `Uri\WhatWg\Url` implementation are not affected by this issue.

### Details

PHP uses the uriparser library to convert an RFC 3986 URI back to text. The vulnerable implementation does not correctly handle the library's output-size limit or errors returned while calculating or writing the result.

For a URI whose string representation is exactly 2,147,483,647 bytes, PHP overflows the size calculation when it reserves space for the terminating byte. The conversion then fails, but PHP can still return the allocated string as a successful result. With longer URIs, PHP can use an incomplete length calculation and return only part of the URI.

Testing on a normal, non-debug PHP build confirmed that `toString()` and `toRawString()` could return a 2,147,483,647-byte string containing zeroes. A URI one byte longer returned only its `a://b/` prefix. Other operations that convert an RFC 3986 URI to text can reach the same implementation.

The defect is in PHP's handling of uriparser's size limit and return values. Updating uriparser alone does not correct it. Correct handling requires PHP to reject a representation that cannot fit the library's supported output size and report a conversion error instead of returning an invalid string.

### Impact

Exploitation requires an application to pass attacker-controlled URI data large enough to reach the approximately 2 GiB boundary to an affected operation. The PHP process must also have enough memory to construct and process the URI. Normal application-level URI length limits prevent the demonstrated inputs from reaching this condition.

An application that trusts the resulting string may make an incorrect comparison, validation or routing decision, or store an incomplete URI. The large allocations can also exhaust the request's memory allowance. In the tested development build, exceeding the soft memory limit produced a memory-exhaustion error; exceeding the hard limit immediately terminated the PHP process. This can temporarily reduce service capacity.

The allocations remain subject to PHP's memory-limit checks. A memory-limit bypass was not observed. The tests also did not establish disclosure of data from other requests: the large result allocation used fresh operating-system memory and contained zeroes. Arbitrary code execution and broader confidentiality or integrity impact have not been demonstrated.

### Affected versions

The affected code was introduced in PHP 8.5.0 together with the `Uri\Rfc3986\Uri` class. PHP 8.4 and earlier do not contain the URI extension and are not affected.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, enforce an appropriate byte-length limit on untrusted URI input before passing it to the affected APIs. Keep the limit well below 2 GiB and account for operations that build or resolve a URI from multiple components. Retain an appropriate PHP memory limit, but do not rely on memory exhaustion as a substitute for validating URI lengths.

summary: Mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs can expose data in plaintext
description:
### Summary

PHP's HTTP and FTP stream wrappers can send data without encryption when an HTTPS or FTPS URL has an uppercase `S` in its scheme, for example `HTTPS://`, `httpS://` or `FTPS://`. Applications using `file_get_contents()`, `fopen()` or other stream functions may therefore expose passwords, authentication tokens, request bodies or transferred files to an attacker able to observe the network traffic.

### Details

The stream wrappers recognise URL schemes without regard to case, but the decision to enable TLS checks for a lowercase `s` at a fixed position. A URL that passes an application's case-insensitive HTTPS or FTPS validation can consequently use the unencrypted HTTP or FTP transport.

The HTTP issue also applies to redirect targets. For example, a `307` redirect from a valid HTTPS connection to an uppercase `HTTPS://` URL can cause the preserved POST body and any retained authentication headers to be sent in cleartext. A request can disclose data even if the destination rejects the unexpected plaintext connection.

The fix determines whether TLS is required by comparing the complete scheme case-insensitively. It covers both the HTTP and FTP stream wrappers.

### Impact

An attacker who can observe an affected connection can read the data that the application expected TLS to protect. This can include Basic authentication credentials, bearer tokens, cookies, sensitive POST data, FTP login credentials and file contents. Exploitation requires an affected URL to reach a stream wrapper, either directly or through a redirect, and access to the resulting network traffic. The impact depends on the data being transferred. disclosure of credentials or other highly sensitive data can have a serious confidentiality impact.

### Affected versions

Mixed-case URLs passed by an application have been affected since PHP 5.2.0, and redirects to a mixed-case URL since PHP 4.3.0. This is based on code inspection.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. As a temporary workaround, ensure that HTTPS and FTPS URL schemes are written in lowercase before passing them to a stream function. If HTTP redirects are allowed, disable automatic redirects and validate and normalise every redirect target before following it. Normalising only the initial URL does not protect requests that follow redirects automatically.

summary: Denial of service through folded HTTP response headers
description:
### Summary

A malicious HTTP server can cause PHP's built-in HTTP stream wrapper to consume excessive CPU while reading a response. Applications using `file_get_contents()`, `fopen()` or other stream functions to fetch an HTTP or HTTPS URL may become slow or unavailable if the response contains a header split across a large number of continuation lines.

### Details

When PHP receives a folded response header, it joins each continuation line to the accumulated header value. The vulnerable implementation allocates a new string and copies the entire value for every line. A response containing many short continuation lines therefore takes disproportionately more time to process as its size grows. PHP performs this work before returning the response body to the application.

This behaviour was introduced by the fix for GHSA-v8xr-gpvj-cx9g (CVE-2025-1217). The new fix accumulates the header in a growing buffer, avoiding a full copy for every continuation line while preserving the existing handling of folded headers.

### Impact

An attacker must control an HTTP response fetched by the application through PHP's built-in HTTP or HTTPS stream wrapper. Enabling `allow_url_fopen` alone does not make an application vulnerable to a remote attack. the attacker must also be able to trigger a suitable outbound request or influence a server that the application already contacts.

Repeated or concurrent requests can keep PHP workers busy and deny service to other users. Testing confirmed that two malicious responses could occupy both workers in a two-worker PHP-FPM pool and temporarily prevent an unrelated request from completing. The demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption. No confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

### Affected versions

The affected code was introduced by the fix for GHSA-v8xr-gpvj-cx9g, first released in PHP 8.1.32, 8.2.28, 8.3.19 and 8.4.5. Earlier versions are not affected.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. Until then, restrict outbound requests to trusted destinations, including redirect targets. An egress proxy that enforces response-header size and count limits can reject malicious responses before PHP processes them. Request execution limits and PHP-FPM's `request_terminate_timeout` can limit how long workers remain occupied, but do not remove the vulnerable parsing behaviour.

summary: Use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown
description:
### Summary

As part of CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp), PHP 8.5.12 fixes a generic use-after-free of the `last_fatal_error_backtrace` global by clearing it during executor shutdown. Further scenarios have been discovered in which a fatal diagnostic during later shutdown work repopulates the global. The request heap is then released, and an early diagnostic in a subsequent request handled by the same worker can access the stale backtrace before normal executor initialization.

### Details

The backtrace can be recreated while PHP restores modified INI settings after executor cleanup:

- When `max_memory_limit` is specified in both the global and a path-specific configuration, restoring the global limit can fail if memory consumption still exceeds that limit. The resulting fatal error recreates the backtrace.
- When the global configuration specifies `zlib.output_compression=1`, and a path-specific configuration specifies `zlib.output_compression=0` and `output_handler=ob_gzhandler` (or another handler), restoring compression before restoring `output_handler` can raise a fatal configuration error because the two settings conflict.

Both shutdown cases are possible with PHP-FPM and mod_php. The `max_memory_limit` override requires administrative configuration. `.user.ini` can supply the zlib settings but cannot change `max_memory_limit`.

Exploitation also requires a diagnostic before executor initialization in a later request handled by the same worker. Apache per-directory configuration can provide this. FPM is conditionally exposed when the frontend sends a diagnostic-producing `PHP_VALUE` or `PHP_ADMIN_VALUE` FastCGI parameter. Ordinary FPM pool settings and `.user.ini` do not provide this early diagnostic.

The fix is generic: PHP no longer creates or consumes the fatal-error backtrace while the executor is inactive. This also covers other shutdown diagnostics that might recreate the same state.

### Impact

Successful exploitation can result in memory corruption and potentially full remote code execution (RCE), as in CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp). The two restoration cases demonstrate heap use-after-free and worker crashes. RCE through these specific entry points has not been demonstrated.

### Affected versions

The affected global was introduced in PHP 8.5.0 by fatal error backtraces. The fix for CVE-2026-109619 in PHP 8.5.12 cleared it during executor shutdown but did not stop later shutdown work from setting it again, so every PHP 8.5 release before 8.5.13 is affected. PHP 8.4 and earlier do not contain the global and are not affected.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13 when it becomes available. As a temporary workaround, disable fatal-error backtraces administratively with `fatal_error_backtraces=0` and restart all workers. Ensure that request-specific configuration cannot re-enable the setting.

summary: Use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown
description:
### Summary

PHP can retain a pointer to a script filename after session shutdown is interrupted and the request memory has been released. A later request handled by the same worker can then release the stale string, causing a heap use-after-free.

This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp). It affects PHP 8.3 and later. PHP 8.2 does not contain the affected session filename field.

### Details

When a session starts, PHP records the executing script's filename in an internal global variable. Session shutdown normally releases this string, but it destroys the session variables first. That destruction can invoke application callbacks, including a user-defined stream wrapper's `stream_close()` method.

A fatal error in such a callback can abort session shutdown before the filename is released or cleared. PHP catches the bailout and continues shutting down the request. The request heap is then freed while the worker still retains the filename pointer.

The next request's session initialization does not reset this field. Starting another session can release the stale string, and ordinary session-module shutdown can also reach it even when the next script does not call any session functions. The requests must reach the same worker, but they do not need to belong to the same user or session.

The reported reproducer uses PHP-FPM with OPcache disabled and a stream resource held in the session. Its close callback raises a fatal error during cleanup. A subsequent request then reaches the freed filename. The report confirms the use-after-free on PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP 8.3.36 contains the same vulnerable code.

Unlike the early-error and upload-progress cases in the original advisory, this path does not require a diagnostic-producing FastCGI parameter or session upload progress.

### Impact

An attacker who can cause an application's session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated. Authentication requirements depend on the application path that reaches the failing cleanup.

The demonstrated configuration has OPcache disabled, so the recorded filename belongs to the request heap. A filename retained in persistent OPcache memory does not produce the same dangling pointer. Exploitability depends on how the affected script was loaded and whether its filename is request-owned.

### Affected versions

The affected field was introduced in PHP 8.3.0, when `session_start()` began recording the file and line where a session was started in order to report them in the notice about an already active session. PHP 8.2 and earlier do not contain the field and are not affected.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. The fix clears the recorded session filename and line number during session initialization. It also terminates the PHP process if a module's request-shutdown handler bails out, preventing the process from handling another request with only partially cleaned-up state.

Until the update is available, avoid fatal errors in callbacks reached during session cleanup. For PHP-FPM, setting `pm.max_requests=1` and restarting the workers prevents the demonstrated sequence from reaching a second request in the same worker, at a performance cost.

Disabling session upload progress does not address this path. Enabling OPcache alone is not a reliable mitigation because scripts can still execute without being cached.

summary: PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free can lead to local privilege escalation
description:
### Summary

PHP-FPM can dispatch an epoll event that refers to a freed worker record when worker output capture is enabled. An attacker who can execute PHP code in an unprivileged FPM worker can exploit this use-after-free to execute commands with the privileges of the FPM master, which commonly runs as root.

### Details

When `catch_workers_output` is enabled, the FPM master monitors pipes connected to worker stdout and stderr. The epoll registrations store pointers to event structures embedded in the corresponding worker record.

When a worker exits, `fpm_child_close()` attempts to drain its output pipes. If a helper process still holds a pipe's write end open, the read can return `EAGAIN` instead of reaching EOF. In this case, the master closes the pipe's read descriptor without first removing its event or invalidating the descriptor number stored in the worker record. Cleanup of that record is deferred for one second.

An attacker can stop a newly forked sibling after it drops to the pool user but before it closes inherited descriptors. The stopped sibling retains the original pipe readers and epoll descriptor, keeping the original watch alive after the master closes its own descriptors. The delayed cleanup can then use a descriptor number that has already been reused, removing the wrong watch or failing to remove the original one before freeing the worker record. A subsequent write to the old pipe makes epoll return a pointer into the freed record.

The master passes that pointer to `fpm_event_fire()`, which reads and calls the event callback. The demonstrated exploit uses the stale output callback to write through a freed logging buffer, corrupt the allocator's free list, and replace the callback with a function that executes a command. Root command execution was reproduced from a `www-data` worker against unmodified PHP 8.5.12 Docker images on Linux arm64 and x86-64. The exploit is dependent on memory layout and process timing. Curl and OPcache were used to obtain memory addresses for the demonstrated chain; they are not required to trigger the underlying epoll use-after-free.

The affected delayed-cleanup path was introduced in PHP 8.1.20 and 8.2.7. The fix unregisters each stdio event while its original descriptor is still valid, closes the descriptor, and sets the stored descriptor to `-1` so that delayed cleanup cannot act on it again.

### Impact

Exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with `catch_workers_output` enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. A root FPM master permits escalation from the pool user to root. If the master runs as an unprivileged user, successful exploitation is limited to that user's privileges. In a container, this grants the master's container privileges and does not by itself establish a container escape.

The underlying descriptor-lifetime error can also close another worker's reused descriptor, disrupt logging or request handling, cause repeated worker respawns, or crash the master. Common affected configurations include the official PHP-FPM Docker images, which enable worker output capture. The default PHP-FPM setting outside such configurations is `catch_workers_output = no`.

### Affected versions

The affected delayed-cleanup path was introduced by the fix for GH-10461, first released in PHP 8.1.20 and 8.2.7.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to the fixed release for your PHP branch when it becomes available. As a temporary workaround, disable `catch_workers_output` in affected pools. Running the FPM master without root limits the privileges obtainable through this vulnerability, but does not correct the use-after-free. Disabling Curl or OPcache only removes parts of the demonstrated exploit chain and should not be treated as a complete mitigation.

summary: RCE via OOM corruption
description:
## Summary

PHP uses `longjmp()` for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. In some contexts, request memory is temporarily reachable before it is fully initialized. If any allocation fails at that point, PHP does not properly account for the early exit and leaves the request memory in an invalid state. The failed allocation does not need to be related to the invalid memory. The request shutdown procedure may then read or branch on it. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).

## Vulnerability

### OOM strategies

Several multipart parsing problems can let a request reach OOM while remaining within its apparent PHP limits:

- A multipart request without a usable declared content length may pass the initial `post_max_size` check and continue supplying decoded body data.
- A multipart part can contain an unrestricted number of headers. Representing these headers inside PHP can use substantially more memory than their wire representation, allowing a request within `post_max_size` to exhaust the normal `memory_limit`.
- Empty file controls do not count towards `max_file_uploads` but still create the normal file metadata arrays. Nested field names multiply the generated array work.

OOM can also be reached in application-specific ways when attacker-controlled input causes a sufficiently large allocation or repeated memory use.

### Susceptibility

Apache mod_php unconditionally invokes the request shutdown procedure, even when request startup has failed. During request startup, automatic body parsing can exhaust the configured memory limit and exit the request in a context where state is temporarily invalid. Shutdown then processes this invalid state. This happens entirely before any application-specific code begins execution.

FPM exits the child when request startup fails. This prevents consumption of the invalid state and removes the child from the pool. After normal startup, OOM may still be reached in a context failing to account for an early exit, with the invalid state being processed during request shutdown. Source analysis therefore supports FPM as susceptible, though no complete FPM exploit has been demonstrated for this SAPI.

Source analysis indicates that FrankenPHP, analogous to Apache mod_php, calls the request shutdown procedure unconditionally, making it likely susceptible to application-independent attacks. LSAPI models FPM, with application-specific exploits being likely but unvalidated.

## Mitigation

The patch removes `longjmp()` for OOM, avoiding an early exit out of contexts that do not properly account for it. It is replaced with a delayed, graceful soft OOM triggered at the next VM safe point, and an immediate hard OOM using `_exit()` if memory consumption reaches a second, higher threshold. The shutdown procedure will no longer see invalid state, and PHP's normal ability to limit memory consumption is retained.

> [!WARNING]
> Updating to a PHP release containing the patch to this vulnerability is the _only_ complete mitigation.

For installations that cannot update, setting and enforcing `memory_limit=-1` administratively is the primary configuration mitigation. It removes the predictable per-request limit that enables the confirmed exploit with a controllable OOM. This is not a complete mitigation. If `mmap()` or another underlying allocation fails, PHP can still use `longjmp()` while incomplete request memory is reachable. Restart every PHP worker and confirm that no pool, directory or application setting restores a finite PHP memory limit.

Keep `post_max_size` conservative and independently enforce the decoded request size at the frontend. Reduce `max_input_nesting_level`, and bound the number of input variables, multipart parts, headers within each part and uploads. These controls reduce hard OOM and denial of service risk even after applying the patch, but do not replace updating. If the application does not use multipart form data, block such requests at the frontend before they reach PHP.

A container or cgroup memory limit (`memory.max`) may provide an alternative to PHP's own `memory_limit` with some limitations. It is not guaranteed to prevent allocation failure and is not a complete mitigation. For example, killing a container or cgroup can also kill the master and every worker, unless each worker has its own group. Killing one FPM child fails only its current requests and FPM's master replaces it quickly. Do _not_ use `RLIMIT_AS` or `RLIMIT_DATA`, as these will cause `mmap()` to fail once the memory limit is reached, triggering the vulnerable `longjmp()` path.

**Important**: Make sure to also follow the remediation advice from the related report.
https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp

## Impact and reliability

The confirmed impact is unauthenticated remote code execution as the web worker account. Complete remote code execution was validated over HTTP against mod_php with default PHP input and memory limits and normal prefork configurations with multiple workers. Additional workers and unrelated traffic can increase the required number of attempts but do not remove the condition. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior and allocator layout.

summary: RCE via stale global state
description:
## Summary

PHP contains various global state, such as error, session, object and extension state that is retained by a worker but points to memory owned by one request. That state must be reset before the request memory is released. Some input, configuration, session and error handling operations run before normal initialization of the next request. They inadvertently access stale state not reset by the previous request before initialization has a chance to replace it, causing a use after free. A strategically crafted heap layout can produce full remote code execution (RCE).

State can survive for more than one reason. A fatal error, including one caused by memory exhaustion, can abandon an operation before it performs its matching reset. A warning or other nonfatal diagnostic can also repopulate error state after that state was already cleared during shutdown. The request heap is then freed while the worker global field still refers to it. A later operation that runs before normal request initialization can consume the stale value.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires both a producer and a consumer. The producer is a PHP operation that stores state owned by one request in a location PHP can access later in a subsequent request. The consumer is a subsequent PHP operation that reads, frees, branches or otherwise acts on the stale state previously stored by the producer.

A concrete vulnerability would arise under the following conditions:

1. A reachable PHP operation stores request-owned state in a globally accessible location, acting as the producer.
2. The state is not reset, or another operation repopulates it after its normal reset.
3. PHP releases the request memory while the persistent worker retains the referring global state.
4. The same worker handles another request.
5. A PHP operation reads, frees, branches or otherwise acts on the stale state before normal request initialization resets it, acting as the consumer.

The demonstrated producing and consuming operations occur in different HTTP requests handled by the same worker. The exact affected versions, configuration and mitigations depend on the internal state affected by the producing operation.

## Vulnerability

### Producers

A producing operation becomes dangerous when its request-owned state remains published after the request heap is freed. A fatal error can cause this by abandoning the operation before it resets the state. Fatal interruptions include parse and compile failures, uncaught errors, failure of `require`, and `Maximum execution time exceeded`.

OOM can provide the same interruption when an affected error, exception, object or extension state was already published.

Even a nonfatal diagnostic from extension or server cleanup during a later shutdown stage can repopulate new request-owned error information to the global state.

### Consumers

There are two confirmed consumers before normal initialization.

#### INI diagnostics before request initialization

A warning, notice or deprecation during initialization can consume stale error state. It does not need to be fatal, displayed or logged. Such a warning may be raised when applying invalid or deprecated INI settings before ordinary executor initialization. Examples include:

- Deterministic deprecations such as `auto_detect_line_endings=1`, a `filter.default` value other than the default, PHP 8.3+ legacy `assert.*` settings, PHP 8.4+ legacy session settings, and PHP 8.5 `report_memleaks=0` or nonzero `intl.error_level`.
- Explicitly configured `mbstring.http_input`, `mbstring.http_output`, `mbstring.internal_encoding`, `iconv.input_encoding`, `iconv.output_encoding` or `iconv.internal_encoding`.
- Invalid or conflicting `zend.assertions`, `memory_limit`, `date.timezone`, DBA, EXIF, mail, OpenSSL, zlib and loaded extension values.
- Malformed or overflowing quantities, including invalid `memory_limit`, body size, input, timeout, stack and extension values on PHP 8.2+.
- Configured log, mail, session or SOAP cache paths rejected under `open_basedir`.

Global state is accessed before PHP decides whether to report, display or log the warning. Changing `error_reporting`, using `@`, or disabling `display_errors` or `log_errors` does not protect against this vulnerability.

##### Reachability

With Apache mod_php, `.htaccess` and Apache `php_value`/`php_flag`/`php_admin_*` directory configuration is applied before `php_request_startup()`. Normal `php.ini` is startup configuration and is not reapplied as a consumer across requests.

FPM is conditionally exposed when nginx, Apache `mod_proxy_fcgi` or another frontend sends `PHP_VALUE`/`PHP_ADMIN_VALUE` parameters that produce a diagnostic before request initialization. FPM pool values are applied when a worker starts, and `.user.ini` is applied after normal initialization. They do not provide the same early consumer. FPM also exits a child after `php_request_startup()` returns failure.

LSAPI can apply special environment INI values early and is a conditional candidate. An equivalent early configuration consumer was not established in the default configuration of FrankenPHP. This does not make this environment immune. It may expose different consumers through application or extension behavior.

#### Session upload progress before normal initialization

Session upload progress can reach session handling before ordinary session initialization. It can therefore consume session or decoder state left by an interrupted request before normal initialization resets it. This consumer is independent of the INI diagnostic path and does not require a diagnostic from configuration.

## Concrete and candidate cases

### PHP 8.5 fatal error backtrace: confirmed

With `fatal_error_backtraces` enabled, fatal error reporting stores backtrace state owned by the request. Resetting of this global state is always missed during shutdown. A diagnostic on a subsequent request reaches the stale value before normal request initialization resets it.

This is the strongest demonstrated case and is the basis of the confirmed mod_php exploitation.

### Session upload progress lifecycle: confirmed

An upload can initialize request-owned session and decoding state before normal module initialization. OOM or another fatal error after that state has been published can prevent its matching reset. PHP then frees the request heap while persistent session or decoder globals still refer to it. A later upload progress operation reaches those globals before ordinary initialization and treats them as valid state.

The demonstrated application-independent trigger is OOM during input processing. Other fatal errors at this stage can cause the same state transition, but generally require additional application, extension or configuration conditions.

With mod_php, both the producing operation and fatal error can occur during multipart startup. FPM terminates a child when this startup fails, so that exact sequence does not survive. The validated FPM path instead publishes state during application execution after successful startup, reaches a fatal error, and then uses session upload progress as the early consumer. It works with a normal dynamic FPM pool, although it depends on a suitable application operation.

Session upload progress is enabled by default, and no application call to `session_start()` is required. It can supply a producer, consumer or both, but exploitation still requires an interruption after state is published and a subsequent request handled by the same worker.

### Other error, exception, object and extension state: conditional

Supported PHP branches contain other request state that may become unsafe after a request boundary. The complete patch resets this wider state because it must not survive into operations that precede normal initialization. Whether it is reachable depends on the application, extensions and the exact point where the state was published.

Fatal errors inside PHP operations that call back into an application deserve particular attention. The callback may introduce a fatal error while the operation still has temporary state. Applicability depends on a route reachable by an attacker, the callbacks registered by that application or extension, and a later consumer before normal request initialization. There is no configuration based mitigation that covers every such operation.

## Mitigation

> [!WARNING]
> Updating to a release containing the complete state reset patch is the only reliable mitigation. **There is no complete generic configuration mitigation as an application, extension or server path may publish stale state or consume it without a predictable log entry.**

For PHP 8.5 installations that cannot update, set `fatal_error_backtraces=0` administratively and restart every worker. This removes the producer used by the confirmed RCE case. It does not cover other request-owned global or extension state.

For the session lifecycle case, set `session.upload_progress.enabled=0` administratively and restart every worker. This prevents the demonstrated early session producing and consuming operations. It does not mitigate the other lifecycle paths. It might be prudent to set `session.upload_progress.enabled=0` if you don't need this feature even after applying the patch, as more attackers try to find flaws in this hardly-used and hardly-tested feature.

Reduce the remaining risk by breaking as many links in the lifecycle as possible:

1. Eliminate fatal errors on paths reachable by an attacker. Include failures that depend on request flow in upload, import, error page, shutdown, destructor, serialization, output handler, plugin and extension paths rather than only failures seen during ordinary page requests.
2. Eliminate warnings and other diagnostics emitted during extension post-deactivation and server cleanup, after normal request error state has already been cleared.
3. Eliminate diagnostics from all INI configuration applied before request initialization. Prefer `php.ini`, FPM pool or server configuration applied at startup over per request overrides, and remove obsolete directives.
4. If performance is not a factor, consider limiting the number of requests a worker may execute using `pm.max_requests=1`.

A PHP execution timeout should be treated like another fatal error. Prevent attacker controlled requests from predictably reaching `Maximum execution time exceeded` while PHP is inside an affected operation. Changing the time limit only removes that possible interruption and does not mitigate the other cases.

### Logging and configuration audit

Enable `log_errors=On`, a functional `error_log`, and `error_reporting=E_ALL` in startup configuration during an isolated audit. Review Apache, PHP-FPM, reverse proxy and service logs for:

- Warnings, deprecations and core errors repeated before target scripts run.
- Warnings and other diagnostics produced during extension or server cleanup.
- Fatal, parse and uncaught error messages.
- `Maximum execution time exceeded`.
- Failures restricted to routes, content types, files, callback implementations or plugin options controlled by an attacker.

Fixing observed errors reduces exposure, but absence of an error in logs is not proof of safety. Historical logs may have been collected with deprecations or other relevant severities excluded. Even an audit using `E_ALL` only covers the routes and application states that were exercised. A failure may also happen before PHP writes the message. Logs must supplement a static configuration and application flow audit.

**Important**: Make sure to also follow the remediation advice from the related report.
https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w

## Impact and reliability

The confirmed impact is unauthenticated heap use-after-free, memory disclosure and remote code execution with the web worker's privileges. The fatal backtrace path has confirmed RCE against mod_php. Session lifecycle RCE was validated against mod_php and FPM. Other state families establish security impact only after a concrete producer and consumer are shown.
